claims.claim: The impersonation rollout decision requires a per-project flag, but the RFC permits enablement only at the system level for all Applications; RFC owner @anandf must change the feature boundary before the rollout can follow the platform decision.

The standing incident rule requires `deletionOrder: AllAtOnce` until the controller fix lands, so the PRD's `deletionOrder: Reverse` workstream cannot proceed to use while that restriction remains; the dev pair reassigned to the progressive sync deletion loop owns clearing this dependency.

The roadmap commits ApplicationSet teardown to manual, one-Application-at-a-time deletion, while the deletion PRD commits to automated `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse` deletion of generated Applications; PRD author @ranakan19 must obtain a roadmap decision before implementation can satisfy both plans.

The hydrator pilot restriction forbids combining pilot repositories with progressive sync until a debounce exists, while T-24578 requests Source Hydrator support specifically to generate Applications whose dependencies are enforced through sync waves; no owner for the required debounce is named, so the T-24578 workstream is blocked on an assumed cross-team dependency.

Reverse deletion depends on `rollingSync.steps` remaining a strictly sequential list, while T-28755 proposes parallel groups inside that structure and the Stable plan freezes the current one-match-set-per-step shape; the Progressive Sync Stable owner must either land parallelism as a new field before Stable or reject it to preserve `deletionOrder: Reverse`.

The rollout decision changes impersonation from the RFC's system-level flag to a per-project flag. On enabled projects, the destination service account acts for sync and diff, Kubernetes audit events record both the requesting and impersonated identities, and the ArgoCD admin must review both the project's destinationServiceAccounts mapping and its flag state; without that project-level enablement evidence, an auditor cannot determine which identity was expected to act.

Server-Side Diff breaks the intended identity boundary: sync acts as the AppProject destinationServiceAccounts service account, while external-cluster diff acts as the cluster Secret credential and accumulates real patch authority. Kubernetes audit therefore attributes diff writes to the standing cluster identity rather than the reviewed impersonated identity, so AppProject admin review does not cover the credential actually authorized for diff and a separate review of cluster Secret RBAC is required.

The namespace-boundary request requires split execution: CreateNamespace and managedNamespaceMetadata must act as the Argo CD control-plane service account, while repository resource sync acts as the destinationServiceAccounts service account with Namespace denied. Kubernetes audit events can evidence the two identities, and the ArgoCD admin must review both the control-plane Namespace grant and the AppProject service-account mapping; reviewing only the impersonated account leaves the privileged namespace action outside the access review.

Hydrated pushes act under the repository-write GitHub App credential, not the human commitAuthor copied into hydrator.metadata; unsigned commits provide no cryptographic actor evidence, while the proposed cluster-wide signing key proves only possession of a Secret readable by other Argo CD components. Access review must therefore cover every identity able to read both repository-write and signing-key Secrets, but neither design names an owner for that review, so a valid signature cannot establish that the commit server performed the push.

provenance-and-authorship: Hydrated-branch records identify the dry commit's human `commitAuthor`, although the GitHub App credential produces the hydrated content; with `commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits` defaulting to `false`, neither the credited human nor the pushing app is cryptographically tied to the hydrated commit, so authorship can only be assumed from copied metadata.

Push-to-stage transfers responsibility for moving fresh manifests to the deployment branch to an external promoter, but the operative stage-branch promoter is an unowned shell script; when it has not promoted fresh output, auto-sync can deploy old hydrated files, leaving no named holder responsible for the automated act that selects the deployed record.

licensed-review: The published roadmap commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and teardown will remain manual, while the deletion PRD specifies `deletionOrder` with `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse`; licensed counsel should determine, under the governing law and customer agreements for each affected jurisdiction, whether shipping the PRD would breach a binding or incorporated published commitment.

The roadmap commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and teardown remains manual, while the Progressive Sync deletion PRD commits to `strategy.deletionOrder` with automated `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse` deletion. The Progressive Sync product owner must decide which scope promise governs.

The impersonation RFC commits that the feature can be enabled or disabled only at system level for all Applications, while the rollout decision requires a per-project flag and explicitly rejects fleet-wide enablement. The impersonation RFC owners and approvers own the call on replacing the system-level commitment.

Parallel progressive sync requires multiple match groups within a concurrent step, but `Reverse` deletion commits to deriving one unambiguous order from strictly sequential `rollingSync.steps`, and Stable promotion will freeze the current one-match-set-per-step shape. The Progressive Sync API owner must decide before Stable whether parallelism gets a new field, Reverse is constrained or redesigned, or the enhancement is rejected.

Progressive Sync's spec-only rollout failure is unobservable in production at fleet scale: support estimates frequency from pings because no counter records `specChanged` without a resulting sync operation, while the open metrics request covers detection-to-trigger time, step duration, ApplicationSet-caused refreshes, and waiting Applications but does not define that counter. Promoting Progressive Sync to Stable therefore lacks a measured pre-promotion failure-rate baseline for a known path that leaves children OutOfSync while `status.applicationStatus` remains Healthy.

The reverse-deletion wave-restart loop is reproducible in staging but unobservable as a production rate: operators can see an individual Application flip between Deleting and Syncing, yet the ticket has no logs and the interim AllAtOnce rule has no controller check or alert. The open Progressive Sync metrics request also lacks a deletion-loop or wave-restart counter, so there is no before/after baseline with which to validate the planned controller fix or detect failures of the manual mitigation.

Hydrator-driven Progressive Sync churn is currently observable only as individual hydrated commits and rollout symptoms, not as a measured causal rate: each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave, while the requested metric for ApplicationSet-caused Application refreshes does not distinguish hydrator commits or count wave restarts. The pilot restriction against combining hydration with Progressive Sync therefore has no baseline for deciding whether a future debounce actually makes that combination safe.

Impersonation diff failures are observable today through CI fatal errors and controller `ComparisonError` events, but there is no aggregate measurement of failures by diff path, destination identity, resource kind, or enabled project. Because the rollout is gated per project until the diff path is fixed, the absence of a failure-rate denominator and pre-enable baseline prevents operators from verifying that diff and sync consistently use `destinationServiceAccounts` before expanding the flag.

T-26271's missing-permissions failure is the observable result of the impersonation design selecting one `defaultServiceAccount` per Application destination and using that identity for kubectl operations: Server-Side Diff's dry-run of cluster-scoped resources therefore inherits an identity designed around namespaced tenant permissions.

T-28695's external-cluster diff identity mismatch exposes the boundary in the impersonation design: `destinationServiceAccounts` is propagated through the Application controller's `SyncContext` for sync, while Server-Side Diff remains on the cluster Secret credential.

T-27833's inability to let `CreateNamespace=true` use the control-plane identity while ordinary resources use a restricted identity follows from the design's per-Application rule: one service account is selected from `Application.spec.destination.namespace` for all resources in the sync operation, not per resource.

T-26443's immediate sync of stale files after `syncSource` changes is the push-to-stage design operating as specified: Argo CD watches `syncSource.targetBranch` for deployment while an external system, not the hydrator, controls when newly hydrated output moves from `hydrateTo` onto that branch.

T-24417's inability to use a Helm-repository chart directly as `drySource` follows from the hydrator decision to permit only one dry source and require the umbrella-chart dependency approach instead of preserving multi-source external chart or values inclusion.

T-27327's need for rollback to write old rendered manifests forward onto the sync branch follows from the hydrator's source-of-truth decision: deployed desired state is the hydrated Git branch, promotion and reversion are performed through Git, and `Application.spec` inputs are deliberately not a complete rendering record.

T-28511's deletion wave restarting while a child remains Progressing is tied to the `Reverse` deletion design, which reverses `rollingSync.steps` and waits for each Application to be fully deleted before advancing to the next.

T-27949's repeated source-change triggers on hydrator pilot repositories follow from the hydrator design's commit model: every detected dry commit produces and pushes a hydrated commit to the configured target branch, which child Applications then observe as a new source revision.

T-28755's proposed parallel match groups alter the exact structure on which `Reverse` deletion depends: the deletion design derives an unambiguous last-in-first-out order from a strictly sequential `rollingSync.steps` list containing one match group per step.

proposals.change: Record that impersonation rollout is controlled per project, not fleet-wide, and must remain disabled until the diff behavior is fixed.
proposals.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed root cause: with impersonation enabled, diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch permission for cluster-scoped resources; the cluster Secret is not the cause.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Record that the history and rollback work is deprioritized until next quarter and its developer pair has moved to the progressive-sync deletion-loop work.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record the resulting exposure: there is no automated rollback if progressive-sync deletion fails midway, potentially leaving the ApplicationSet inconsistent with the cluster.
proposals.citedLine: Because the hydrator rollback work was deprioritized, there is no automated mechanism to revert manifest changes if the progressive sync deletion logic fails mid-way, creating a potential state where the application set is inconsistent with the cluster.

proposals.change: Record that the delete/recreate loop was reproduced in staging with reverse deletion order and document the temporary runbook mitigation: switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before manually deleting a child Application.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record that the AllAtOnce workaround is manual and lacks a controller check or alert, leaving operators able to trigger the wave-restart loop through reverse-order deletion on hydrated repositories.
proposals.citedLine: The operational rule to switch to AllAtOnce deletion is a manual mitigation; without a controller-level check or alert, operators might inadvertently use the reverse deletion order on hydrated repos, triggering the wave-restart loop that causes rolling sync instability.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed hydrator interaction and pilot restriction: every hydrator push restarts the rolling-sync wave, so hydrator pilot repositories must not use progressive sync until debounce exists.
proposals.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

deltas.body: Impersonation rollout is per-project rather than fleet-wide, and no project may enable it until the diff behavior is fixed.
